transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lynda Kenyon. President Trump is campaigning in Georgia today while former President Obama hits the campaign trail in Michigan after an appearance in Ohio to rally support for Democrats ahead of the November midterms. Michigan Public Radio's Colin Jackson reports.
As have been on Michigan all election cycle, thanks in part to its neck-and-neck U.S. Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers has been trying to chip away at Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's base by targeting black voters, especially in Detroit.
Strategist Alexis Wiley says the most important thing Obama can do in Detroit this weekend is show unequivocal support for El-Sayed.
Having President Obama's seal of approval is a huge deal, and it's going to go a long way for Abdul. He's going to benefit the most from this weekend.
Both major parties see Michigan's open Senate seat as must-win on the path to a majority. Republicans get their own star power boost Sunday with a visit from President Donald Trump.
For NPR News, I'm Kallen Jackson. The State Department is moving some diplomats out of the Middle East amid new concerns about possible attacks from Iran, as well as ongoing threats from the Houthis in Yemen. NPR's Michelle Kellerman has the latest.
The Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton, says the administration has received information that Iran has "substantially increased efforts" to target U.S. personnel. He tells Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a memo that the plots have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.
The State Department confirmed the unclassified memo and said that the new intelligence is informing staffing adjustments at its embassies. Earlier this week, some diplomats and family members were evacuated from the U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia because of attacks from Yemen. Michelle Kellerman, NPR News.
Clashes erupted in Paris today amid mass protests around the country. NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports the march had been largely peaceful through most of the day.
Protesters of all ages and backgrounds, students, workers, members of the Yellow Vest movement, coerced down a Paris boulevard. Many held signs against capitalism and President Emmanuel Macron.
There were chants against the police and for taxing the rich. Nurse Jenny Bartelemy says things are going downhill in every way.
People are eating so poor and our children have been beaten up by the police and all that. So we just say stop.
TV footage showed skirmishes and tear gas in other cities such as Lyon, Marseille and Toulouse, where protesting was banned. Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
Police report nearly 1,000 arrests in France. The Interior Ministry reported more than 400,000 protesters nationwide. You're listening to NPR News.
Research rockets lifted off over Fairbanks, Alaska this week. So look at the afterlives of dying stars. Shelby Herbert of Alaska Public Media reports the NASA experiment is also zooming in on something much smaller, the dust given off by those stars.
Two rockets pierced thick snow clouds above Alaska. The first looked at a nebula left behind by a dying star, Messier 27. The second carried a tiny lab that recreated the extremely hot, gravity-free conditions inside the nebula that make the tiny grains of dust that make up the universe. NASA scientist Joe Nooth heads up that project.
If the growth process is efficient, what you make are the equivalent of big rocks. Nooth says the study could further scientific understanding of the dust produced by volcanic eruptions and coal-fired power plants, of which Alaska has both.
For NPR News, I'm Shelby Herbert in Fairbanks. Six Flags says it will add seatbelts on the Georgia roller coaster where a rider fell to his death earlier this month. The announcement comes less than two weeks after the 42-year-old man from Atlanta was ejected from his seat on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags over Georgia.
The CEO of Six Flags Entertainment says other roller coasters with a similar restraint system to Goliath's will also get seatbelts. The company currently has eight additional coasters with similar restraints that are shut down at five parks in the U.S. and Canada.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News.
